articles.title: Paracetamol overdose Newport student makes miraculous recovery
articles.summary: Riley Lubas took two over-the counter medicines without realising they both contained paracetamol.
articles.body:
The parents of a student who suffered organ failure and nearly died after accidentally overdosing on paracetamol have spoken of the distress it caused and said they have "no idea how it happened so quickly".

Riley Lubas, 20, came down with a bad cold in March 2025 in his first year at university, and took two over-the counter medicines without realising they both contained paracetamol.

After being placed on life support and enduring weeks in hospital, he went on to make a miraculous recovery, and has even relearned how to walk and talk.

The Royal College of General Practitioners Cymru Wales advised people to always "read the label carefully" and seek advice from a GP before taking medication.

Riley was studying creative media at the University of Bath when he got hit with a springtime cold which he described as feeling "pretty non-eventful".

"People get freshers flu or colds all the time in first year, so I got two medicines," he said.

"I didn't realise at the time that both had paracetamol in them."

A paracetamol overdose can cause severe liver and kidney damage, according to the NHS , with early symptoms often including nausea or vomiting and stomach.

Riley decided to phone for help when his stomach started hurting.

Tests at Bath's Royal United Hospital discovered that his liver was struggling.

His parents, Chris, 40 and Kate Lubas, 39, raced from Newport to be with their son.

Chris, a company director, said doctors were initially concerned it was hepatitis .

"Hours later, at half one in the morning, I got a call from the ICU staff at the hospital saying we had to get there immediately," he added.

"All they could say at the time was they were doing everything they could."

His parents were told Riley was heading towards liver failure, and they watched as his condition deteriorated to the point where he was delirious and hallucinating.

"By 6pm that night, he was sedated and on life support and dialysis and in multiple organ failure," said Chris.

"The staff there were able to finally tell us how bad it had gotten."

Riley's brain fluid had left the hospital staff "concerned" and his lungs and kidneys had also stopped working.

"We were so distressed and had no idea how this could have happened so quickly," Chris added.

By now Riley's condition had become so bad, he was transferred to London's King's College Hospital which has a specialist ICU init.

His parents were asked about his paracetamol intake, and they were able to find the two medications and work out what had happened.

Chris said: "It didn't necessarily help with a solution, but it was good to know the cause at last."

While Riley waited for a liver transplant, doctors began to notice improvements in his health, despite his parents initially being told the damage could be "irreversible".

"They spotted some improvement in the liver," said Chris.

"We watched Riley's situation closely for a couple of days, and he continued to improve, until he was taken off dialysis and life support just a week later."

Riley had to relearn how to walk and talk, spending a total of six weeks at King's College Hospital, before moving to an ICU in Newport.

"We were amazed to see his improvement,' said Chris.

"He'd had a tracheostomy , so he needed to learn how to speak again, and because of how many organs shut down, had to relearn walking too.

"But just seeing him up and alive again was unbelievable."

Chris said there was "no exact answer" that explains his recovery, but doctors think his health and age played a part.

Riley has now recovered and is back working in a pub as a bartender.

His parents have done a 31 miles (50km) hike across the Gower Peninsula to raise money for King's College ICU and raise awareness for paracetamol overdose.

Riley said it was "mad how quickly it all escalated".

He added: "Because I was already sick, when my stomach hurt I just assumed I'd caught a stomach bug, so I didn't notice the pain in my liver specifically.

"I'm just so grateful that I was able to come out the other end alright."

The Office for National Statistics latest figures show there were 27 deaths registered in Wales in 2024 that mentioned any paracetamol on the death certificate.

Dr. Will Mackintosh, a GP and chairman of RCGP Cymru Wales, said accidental paracetamol overdose in young people was "a fairly rare occurrence", but there was a small risk if some inadvertently takes two products containing paracetamol at the same time.

Mackintosh said pressures placed on young people who are working and studying, in particular, can lead to them taking as much over the counter to "keep going when they're ill".

"Particularly things like viral illnesses, while they're not serious, it's important to get enough rest as well," he added.

Mackintosh said he felt rest was sometimes "downplayed" in favour of taking medicine that will get you back to normal as quickly as possible.

"For a lot of these illnesses, you need some time to rest and allow them to run their course as well as taking over the counter medicine," he added.

He said local community pharmacies are "very cautious" about selling large amounts of medication, so they will "often place restrictions on the amount of paracetamol that can be sold".

He said GPs had also become more aware of the risk a paracetamol overdose can have on older patients who, in particular, have low body weight.

"When these things happen, the symptoms can be very severe and the risks are high, so we want to minimise this to as few cases as possible," he added.

He advised people to read the labels carefully and seek advice from your pharmacist or GP, as well as the NHS website.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line .

articles.title: World’s most contagious virus hits major US airport as officials warn of possible exposure
articles.summary: Philadelphia International Airport is tied to a second measles exposure event across multiple terminals amid Pennsylvania's worsening measles outbreak.
articles.body: The City of Philadelphia is reporting two possible measles exposures within a week — the latest at Philadelphia International Airport. The exposure took place at airport terminals B and F, as well as areas used to connect to other terminals in C, D and E, on Sunday, Sept. 13, from 7:45 p.m. to Monday, Sept. 14 at 12:05 a.m., according to the Philadelphia Department of Public Health. The individual with measles was traveling through Philadelphia and did not leave the airport. Health officials encouraged those who were potentially exposed to check their vaccination status and watch for symptoms. MEASLES-INFECTED TRAVELER MAY HAVE EXPOSED PASSENGERS AT LAX AND NEARBY HOTEL, HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN This was the second reported measles exposure in the Philadelphia area, after the first case reported on Sept. 17 at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP). The incident occurred on Sept. 11 at the following locations. The Pennsylvania and Philadelphia health departments, as well as CHOP, reported that they are "working closely to ensure potentially exposed infants receive a preventative antibody product to prevent or lessen severe disease and to take steps to prevent the further spread of measles." MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL In the second news release, Health Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson wrote that this week’s measles exposures are "a reminder of how important it is for all of us to be up to date on our vaccinations." "Every Philadelphian who is fully vaccinated has little to fear from the situation at CHOP and the airport," she said. "Even more importantly, every one of those people is doing their part to help protect our most vulnerable from measles. With outbreaks continuing in Pennsylvania and other places, this is even more important." The health department advised that anyone who has been exposed who is not immune, is unsure of their vaccination status, is an infant, is pregnant and not immune, or is immunocompromised should contact their doctor. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Some people may still be eligible for treatment after exposure that can prevent measles or reduce the severity of illness," the department wrote. "Anyone who develops symptoms should call ahead before visiting a healthcare facility and tell the provider about the possible measles exposure." In August, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania confirmed two measles-related deaths, marking the first losses related to the virus within the state in 35 years. The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed that both Lancaster County individuals were unvaccinated. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Measles is a highly contagious virus that can be fatal in one to three patients per 1,000 cases, data shows. The virus can cause long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Nearly 20% of individuals who contract measles are hospitalized. Measles spreads when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, spreading the virus through respiratory droplets. It can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the person leaves the area, experts caution. articles.title: Granddaughter says grandma rejected MAID before lethal procedure, ‘I don’t want the death shot’
articles.summary: Brigitte Stegemann's granddaughter alleges the 83-year-old had no idea she was about to die until she was told a lethal MAID injection was scheduled.
articles.body: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800-273-TALK (8255). The granddaughter of an 83-year-old Canadian woman who died through the country’s assisted-death program in July says her grandmother had no idea she was about to die until she was told she would be given a lethal injection just days prior. Brigitte Kranendonk, who cared for her grandmother Brigitte Stegemann, says the family cut short a vacation after learning that the long-term care home had scheduled a second MAiD assessment, despite Stegemann previously declining the procedure. "Just before we had come back from our vacation, I received a phone call from the home stating that they had booked a second assessment for MAiD to happen with my grandmother, and at this point my Oma had already denied MAiD," Kranendonk told Fox News Digital in an interview Tuesday. "When we went to the home after our vacation – we did cut it short, we came home, we saw her. She had no idea what was happening." DEMENTIA STOLE MY GRANDMOTHER FROM US. I AM FIGHTING TO GIVE FAMILIES MORE TIME Kranendonk said that she was her grandmother’s primary caregiver and that her family had decided to place Stegemann at The Pearl care home in Cannifton due to physical and mental decline. Her grandmother, however, still had a good appetite and was in good spirits even following a stomach cancer diagnosis, and rejected the idea of using MAiD when it was presented as an option. "She had an opportunity to get an IV port, meaning for injectable medicine. They didn't have to re-poke her every time," Kranendonk said. "It was kind of a one-and-done deal. She had ripped it out several times because she kept saying, ‘I don't want the death shot.’" "And it wasn't until I, face to face, explained it to her that this is not what it is, this is just pain management," Kranendonk added. "That was the scary part is that it felt like she went from screaming, 'I don't want the death shot,' to then accepting MAiD. But only while I was on vacation." EXCLUSIVE: ‘BROKEN COUNTRY’ FILMMAKER WARNS CANADA’S SLOW DECLINE OFFERS CAUTIONARY TALE FOR AMERICANS Stegemann was killed under Canada’s physician-assisted suicide program, called Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD), on July 10. Kranendonk says her grandmother’s first language was not English and that she was severely hearing impaired. "My grandmother's first language is not English," Kranendonk said. "She is severely hearing impaired. And she, her whole life, was terrified of feeling dumb. She never wanted to look as if she didn't understand what was going on. And so when the doctor came in and was explaining MAiD and using very loose terms, like, ‘We're just going to give you medicine, you're not going to feel pain. And don't worry, you won't have a bowel movement,’ my grandma's just sitting there nodding. And I stopped, and I said to her, ‘She doesn't understand what you're saying.’" When Kranendonk directly asked Stegemann whether she knew she would die that Friday, she said her grandmother was visibly shocked and cried for roughly 45 minutes, repeatedly saying, "I made a mistake." NEW YORK NUNS WILL NOT BE FORCED TO COMPLY WITH ASSISTED-SUICIDE LAW WHILE CASE PROGRESSES The doctor had allegedly said Stegemann could "deny" MAiD on the day of the procedure, but Stegemann was already unsure if her grandmother had actually consented to it in the first place. The day the procedure occurred, Kranendonk said the nurse who was administering the IV was not wearing gloves and had a hard time putting it into her right arm, piercing her grandmother many times. "I'm not a nurse," Kranendonk said. "I've never done an IV. I've seen them done before. There was so much blood with this IV. It was all over her arm, it was soaking through her nighty, it was all over the pillow. And it was all over the nurse's hands. And at that moment when I saw all the blood all over the nurse's hands, I realized the nurse was not even wearing gloves." Kranendonk also alleges that Stegemann did not verbally acknowledge the doctor’s final question before the procedure was started. NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS "And the doctor comes in and says, I can't remember exactly how she worded it, but it was something like, ‘Good morning, Brigitte, are you OK if we proceed with MAiD,’ or, ‘Are you OK if we proceed?’ I can't remember what she asked my Oma. My Oma doesn't say anything. No acknowledgment, no head nod, nothing. Just lying there with her eyes closed. And the doctor says, ‘OK, we're going to proceed.’" Kranendonk said the family is seeking investigations by the coroner’s office, an ombudsman and the long-term care action line. ASSISTED LIVING CENTER SENT RESIDENT TO DOCTOR'S APPOINTMENT AFTER GIVING HIM 18 SHOTS, 5 AM BEER: OFFICIALS "With the investigation with the coroner's office, the ombudsman, the long-term care action line, there's essentially two streams here that we're asking to be investigated under," Kranendonk said. "One is the part of the home, and the part that the home had played in this, and then also the MAiD process. The home had taken it upon themselves to fill out the paperwork, witness and get my Oma to sign off. I don't know what the conversation was that they had with her while she was signing the paperwork, I don't know if she even knew that it was the MAiD paperwork for it." On its website, The Pearl care home in Cannifton, where Stegemann lived, says that it currently has 57 licensed beds with 86 people on the waiting list. articles.title: Trump administration cuts ACA coverage for 750,000 people it says were ‘fraudulently’ enrolled
articles.summary: The Trump administration is removing hundreds of thousands of enrollees from Obamacare plans, claiming that many were receiving subsidies they didn’t qualify for and that some did not even exist.
articles.body: The Trump administration is removing hundreds of thousands of enrollees from Affordable Care Act plans, claiming that many were receiving subsidies they didn’t qualify for and that some did not even exist. The announcement is the latest effort by the administration to argue that fraud has inflated ACA enrollment, even as experts question the scale of the alleged fraud. Vice President JD Vance and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz — who have teamed up on a broader push to root out fraud in government health programs — said Tuesday that roughly 750,000 people have had their ACA coverage canceled. The administration did not provide details about who lost coverage or how those individuals were informed. The cuts, Vance said, would save U.S. taxpayers $2.2 billion. “These programs are deserving, they are important, but they’re not going to exist unless we stop the fraud,” Vance said at a news conference. During the Biden administration, ACA enrollment increased from about 11 million to a record 24 million, when pandemic-era enhanced tax credits expanded who was eligible for subsidies. ACA enrollment declined by roughly 3 million people this year after those enhanced subsidies expired, making monthly premiums significantly more expensive for millions of people. In an interview with NBC News in March, Oz claimed that some of the enrollment increase — around 4 million to 5 million — has been driven by fraud, particularly by insurance brokers, who help people find and sign up for health plans. He said some brokers enrolled people without their knowledge to collect commission fees from insurers. In other cases, Oz said, people’s incomes made them ineligible for receiving subsidies, they had mistakenly signed up for duplicate plans or they did not exist at all. “In fact, the fact that we have 23 million makes me think we have too many participants in the ACA,” Oz said at the time. “It’s too high of a number.” Oz reiterated his claim during the news conference Tuesday, saying, “Obamacare had 10 million enrollees from 2015 to 2020. During Covid, it went up to 22 million people.” “So the question becomes, what happened?” he said. “Well, the guardrails were weakened, and the prior administration decided not to enforce the weakened guardrails.” Oz said the administration looked at a combination of factors it considered suspicious. The people had been enrolled with the help of a broker or agent, had never filed a claim, had their entire monthly premium covered by federal tax credits, and either had no Social Security number or immigration documents that the CMS could verify in real time. “We call them phantoms, because we believe most of them don’t exist or they had no idea they had coverage,” he said. “We believe that because we’ve been writing them, telexing them, FedExing, whatever we possibly can do to get in touch with them. They won’t answer.” It’s unclear whether the enrollees who lost their coverage were paying their premiums. Health policy experts say fraud exists in the ACA, as well as the entire U.S. healthcare system. In 2025, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that 2.3 million people were improperly receiving enhanced tax credits. Experts, however, question how widespread the fraud in the program is — and whether the administration is overstating its role in the ACA’s enrollment increases. Much of the enrollment decline, experts say, isn’t due to eliminating fraud but because coverage became unaffordable after the end of the enhanced tax credits. “It is entirely possible that many of these people were enrolled without their knowledge or were so-called phantom enrollees,” said Cynthia Cox, director of the program on the ACA at KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group. “It is also entirely possible that many of these people were legitimately enrolled and simply did not respond in time.” Vance said that the administration is also investigating an additional 419,000 people it says may be improperly enrolled. “They had something about their story that was a little bit different than what we expected from the 100% fraud story,” Oz said at the news conference. “We’re giving them another chance.”

articles.title: Popular weight-loss drugs face numerous lawsuits over rare ‘eye stroke’ linked to vision loss
articles.summary: Hundreds of consumers allege GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy caused NAION, a rare eye stroke linked to sudden, often permanent vision loss.
articles.body: Hundreds of consumers are suing the manufacturers of GLP-1 receptor agonists, alleging the medications may increase the risk of a rare form of vision loss. The patients behind the lawsuits allege that the medications caused NAION (nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy), according to The Wall Street Journal. NAION is a rare eye condition in which blood flow to the optic nerve is suddenly reduced, leading to sudden vision loss. POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER It is the most common cause of acute optic nerve injury in adults over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology and the National Eye Institute, which describes it as an "eye stroke." "The problem with NAION is there's no treatment," Dr. Douglas Lazzaro, an ophthalmologist at NYU Langone Health, told Fox News Digital. "So it can cause some very profound vision loss." The companies in question, Novo Nordisk (maker of Ozempic and Wegovy) and Eli Lilly (maker of Mounjaro and Zepbound), have disputed the allegations, according to the WSJ report. POPULAR ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION DRUG LINKED TO EYE DISEASE THAT CAN CAUSE IRREVERSIBLE VISION LOSS Novo Nordisk called the lawsuits meritless and pointed to company-funded research finding no increased risk of NAION with its drugs. Eli Lilly said it continues to monitor safety data and maintained that current studies do not prove GLP-1 medications cause the condition. Fox News Digital reached out to the companies requesting comment. What the research suggests Most of the published research to date has examined semaglutide, rather than tirzepatide. In a data analysis of 37 million adults published in JAMA Ophthalmology in 2025, researchers found that people using semaglutide experienced a modest increase in NAION risk compared to people taking SGLT2 inhibitors, another class of diabetes medication. DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS A 2024 Harvard Medical School study, published in the same journal, found that patients with type 2 diabetes who were prescribed semaglutide had approximately a fourfold higher relative risk of developing NAION. The absolute risk remained very low. The authors of both studies noted that the research was observational and could not prove that the medication caused NAION. They emphasized that more evidence is needed. The FDA has said it is reviewing available evidence regarding a possible association between semaglutide and NAION. The agency has not concluded that semaglutide causes NAION and has not issued a safety warning for semaglutide medications. The European Medicines Agency concluded there is sufficient evidence of a possible association to recommend adding NAION as a "very rare" adverse reaction to semaglutide product information in Europe. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Lazzaro agreed that "whether or not that's statistically significant is hard to assess, because there were so many variables in this and it's hard to exactly match patients." "But when they removed all of what they felt were confounding variables… how obese were the patients, male versus female, age, hypertension, level of obesity… they did find that there was a higher risk of NAION." What to know about NAION NAION typically causes sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, per the AAO. Other symptoms may include blurred or dim vision, loss of peripheral vision or decreased color vision. Symptoms tend to develop first thing in the morning after waking up. The biggest risk factors for the condition include age, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obstructive sleep apnea and smoking. As many people taking GLP-1 drugs have diabetes or obesity, some of these underlying risk factors could be factors in vision issues, experts note. Diabetes itself is a well-established risk factor for NAION, making it difficult for observational studies to separate the effects of the disease from those of the medication, experts have noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Vision loss from NAION is often permanent. While some patients may regain partial vision over time, there is no proven treatment that can reverse the optic nerve damage. The condition is rare, with roughly two to 10 cases per 100,000 people each year, depending on the population studied. Experts emphasize that patients should not stop taking a prescribed GLP-1 medication without first speaking with their healthcare provider. For many people with diabetes or obesity, the medications' proven benefits may outweigh any potential vision risk. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ When discussing NAION, one important factor is what doctors call a "disc at risk," referring to certain characteristics of the optic disc, or optic nerve. "So if I had a patient who had what I would see on exam is a disk at risk, a very compact optic nerve where everything's crowded, I would tell that patient probably to not go on a semaglutide," Lazzaro advised. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "My overall take on the matter is there's probably a slightly increased risk of NAION when using the semaglutides, but I think the health benefits outweigh the risks," he went on. "And unless I have a patient with a disk at risk, I would probably tell them to go on them if they're going to be a lot healthier from an overall standpoint."

articles.title: 'Peeing a jellyfish': Children's ketamine injuries revealed
articles.summary: Doctors running the UK's first and only dedicated NHS clinic for children with ketamine bladder say they are seeing patients as young as 13.
articles.body:
Children as young as 13 are getting ketamine bladder damage, doctors running the UK's first and only dedicated NHS clinic for it have told the BBC in an exclusive interview.

Medics at Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool say some patients - they have had over 100 referrals since opening last May - describe 'peeing a jellyfish', which is some of the bladder's protective lining being shed.

Prolonged damage can lead to incontinence or uncontrolled peeing, and even kidney failure.

Many children at the clinic had been taking ketamine for a year or more, meaning some may have started when they were 12 or younger.

Some with emotional trauma say the ketamine, sold for pocket money prices, helps "shush" or quieten their brain.

The drug is a general anaesthetic so it reduces or blunts sensations in the body.

Users say it can make them feel dream-like and detached, chilled and relaxed.

Prof Rachel Isba who runs the clinic told the BBC some of the children she has seen had started wetting the bed or having to go to the toilet more often and in a hurry.

"Sometimes they don't always make it. They might have accidents...and a lot of them report pain in their bladder.

"They describe this feeling of weeing over broken glass. It's very painful."

She says, unfortunately, some of them will use the ketamine to treat the pain.

"Ketamine is a very good pain reliever. It's an anaesthetic, and so they get into a vicious cycle or 'K loop', which makes their bladder worse," says Isba.

She says ketamine is very cheap, "pocket-money level".

"And you only need a small amount to feel an effect."

She says some children find it hard to quit if their mates are still doing it.

"There's use going on at school. That's really difficult. And, unfortunately for many of these children they are not able to attend education for various reasons."

Some had pre-existing conditions like ADHD, while others had been in and out of the care system.

Ketamine abuse in children and young people is on the rise in the UK.

The Alder Hey doctors saw one young patient in 2023, nine in 2024, and then "a rapid escalation" in 2025, which led them to open the bespoke clinic in May.

They get about one referral every week from GPs or emergency departments in Cheshire, Merseyside and other nearby regions.

Of the first 60 they saw, 43 were girls.

Despite its name, "ketamine bladder" can affect the entire urinary tract, including the kidneys and ureters.

Symptoms include an urgent and frequent need to urinate. This can be very painful and the pee can be blood-stained.

Although stopping using ketamine can help, sometimes the damage can be so serious that the bladder needs surgical repair or even removal.

Some users experience abdominal pain and spasms, or "K cramps" too.

There are reports that heavy users are getting liver damage, but it is difficult to separate harms from other things people may also be taking, including other street drugs and alcohol.

Isba says cannabis and alcohol are still more popular, but ketamine is "probably up into third place".

Children at the clinic often say they have also tried other drugs, drank alcohol, and vaped.

About three out of every 10 people who frequently use ketamine get bladder issues, says the British Association of Urological Surgeons .

Sometimes it is reversible, if the drug use stops.

Given the risks, there have been calls to reclassify it as a Class A drug - like cocaine and heroin - but the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs has recommended to government that ketamine should remain a Class B controlled substance, like amphetamines and cannabis.

Isba says children are disadvantaged when it comes to accessing services.

"There are definitely some children out there who are under the age of 16 who if they were 18 would be offered an inpatient detox stay. But because we don't have those facilities in the UK, they are not able to access that and that feels unfair. Particularly for the ones who are ready to stop."
